subject: biology

items.q: Which statement about homeostasis in humans is correct?
items.correct: Blood glucose concentration fluctuates within narrow preset limits around a set point.
items.misconception: Core body temperature is held at exactly 37 °C with no variation at all.
items.why: GCSE and MYP definitions say homeostasis keeps conditions 'constant', and textbook graphs are often drawn as a flat line at the set point, so students expect zero variation and read normal oscillation as a fault. Homeostasis is the maintenance of the internal environment within preset limits despite fluctuations in the external environment. Body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose concentration and blood osmotic concentration all rise and fall a little around their set points; negative feedback keeps the oscillation small, it does not abolish it.
items.specStatementText: What homeostasis keeps steady
items.random_wrong: Skin temperature is kept within preset limits whatever the air temperature.

items.q: A person's core temperature was recorded at intervals through a day on which the air temperature ranged from 5 °C to 30 °C. The readings were 36.6, 36.9, 37.2, 36.8 and 37.1 °C. What do these readings show?
items.correct: Core temperature is being kept within preset limits despite large changes in the external environment.
items.misconception: The readings cannot show homeostasis: skin temperature, not the core, is what is kept within limits.
items.why: The word 'environment' in the definition is read as the surroundings rather than the internal environment, and students have not separated variables that are regulated by feedback from variables that merely change. Homeostasis concerns the internal environment: the composition and conditions of the blood and tissue fluid. The guide's named human examples are body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose concentration and blood osmotic concentration; skin temperature is allowed to vary widely precisely so that core temperature can stay within limits.
items.specStatementText: What homeostasis keeps steady
items.random_wrong: Homeostasis has failed, because the core temperature was not held at one constant value through the day.

items.q: Why are homeostatic variables controlled by negative feedback rather than by positive feedback?
items.correct: Negative feedback opposes a change, returning the variable towards its set point.
items.misconception: Negative feedback responds to harmful changes, while positive feedback responds to beneficial ones.
items.why: The everyday meanings of 'positive' and 'negative' as good and bad are carried into biology, and positive feedback is met first in dramatic contexts such as childbirth, which sound like useful body processes. The terms describe the direction of the response relative to the change, not its value to the organism. Negative feedback reverses a change, which is exactly what maintaining a set point requires. Positive feedback increases a change, which is useful only for processes that must run to completion, such as the contractions of childbirth, and would be catastrophic for temperature or glucose control.
items.specStatementText: Why negative feedback, not positive
items.random_wrong: Negative feedback lowers a variable that has risen, which is the usual direction of deviation.

items.q: During a long run, a person's blood glucose concentration falls to 3.5 mmol L−1. Glucagon secretion increases and the concentration returns to 5 mmol L−1. Which description of this sequence is correct?
items.correct: Negative feedback correcting a fall of the variable below its set point.
items.misconception: Positive feedback, because the response raised the variable, not lowered it.
items.why: The word 'negative' is read as 'decrease', and many taught examples (a thermostat switching a heater off, insulin lowering glucose) show only the correction of a rise, so students assume a rise is the only deviation that negative feedback handles. 'Negative' refers to the response opposing the change, whatever its direction. A fall in blood glucose is corrected by glucagon and a rise by insulin; both are negative feedback because each response reverses the deviation. Positive feedback amplifies a change and has no role in returning a variable to its set point.
items.specStatementText: Why negative feedback, not positive
items.random_wrong: Positive feedback, because the response was beneficial and restored health.

items.q: Blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. What happens next?
items.correct: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin into the blood, and target cells take up more glucose.
items.misconception: The hypothalamus detects the rise and sends nerve impulses telling the pancreas to release insulin.
items.why: Thermoregulation, with the hypothalamus as controller, is often taught in the same unit and used as the template for every homeostatic loop, so students insert a brain 'control centre' where the guide places none. In blood glucose regulation the receptor and the effector controller are the same cells. Beta cells and alpha cells of the pancreatic islets monitor the glucose concentration of the blood flowing past them and secrete insulin or glucagon directly in response. The nervous system can modulate this but is not part of the core loop the guide describes.
items.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
items.random_wrong: Insulin is released into the blood, where it breaks down the excess glucose molecules.

items.q: Insulin is secreted into the blood, yet only cells such as liver, skeletal muscle and adipose cells respond to it. Why?
items.correct: Insulin reaches every tissue, but only these cells have receptors that bind it.
items.misconception: Insulin is carried by the blood directly to these organs and to no other part of the body.
items.why: Diagrams draw an arrow from the gland to the target organ, and nerves are taught alongside hormones as the other 'messaging' system, so students assume the same point-to-point delivery. Hormones are transported in the blood to all tissues; there is no directed route. Target specificity comes from receptors: liver, muscle and adipose cells carry insulin receptors and respond, while cells without them are bathed in the same insulin and ignore it. This is also why the whole body's glucose uptake, not one organ's, is affected.
items.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
items.random_wrong: Insulin breaks down glucose only in tissues where glucose is concentrated.

items.q: Which option correctly pairs a hormone with its effect on target cells?
items.correct: Glucagon: liver cells hydrolyse glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
items.misconception: Glycogen: liver cells release glucose when its concentration in the blood falls too low.
items.why: The two words differ by only a few letters and are met together in the same lesson, so they are stored as one blurred term; whichever one is recalled is given the role that the question seems to need. Glucagon (hormone) is secreted by alpha cells of the pancreatic islets, travels in the blood and acts on liver cells. Glycogen (polysaccharide) is the glucose store inside liver and muscle cells. Glucagon stimulates the hydrolysis of glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood.
items.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
items.random_wrong: Insulin: enzymes in the blood plasma digest glucose so that its concentration falls.

items.q: What is the physiological change that underlies type 2 diabetes?
items.correct: Target cells respond less to insulin.
items.misconception: Beta cells are destroyed by the immune system.
items.why: At GCSE diabetes is often introduced through type 1 and the single idea 'no insulin', so students file both types under 'insulin shortage' and treat the numbering as severity rather than as a different mechanism. Type 1: the immune system destroys beta cells, so insulin is not secreted. Type 2: insulin is secreted but target cells no longer respond normally (insulin resistance) because of changes in receptors and signalling, usually linked to obesity and inactivity. This is why type 2 can often be treated by diet and exercise, and why insulin injections are not the first treatment.
items.specStatementText: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
items.random_wrong: Beta cells are damaged by dietary sugar.

items.q: A lean 12-year-old develops very high blood glucose within a few weeks; antibodies against pancreatic islet cells are found in the blood and blood insulin is very low. A 55-year-old with obesity has had slowly rising fasting blood glucose for years, with a high blood insulin concentration. Which interpretation is best supported?
items.correct: The child has type 1 diabetes from autoimmune loss of beta cells; the adult has type 2, with insulin secreted but target cells resistant to it.
items.misconception: The child's diabetes must have been caused by a sugary diet, because it appeared in childhood; the adult's by the ageing of the pancreas.
items.why: Public health messages about diabetes almost all concern type 2 and its diet-related risk factors, and the word 'diabetes' is used for both, so the lifestyle explanation is transferred to type 1. The risk factors differ. Type 1 is linked to genetic predisposition and possibly to viral triggers of the autoimmune response, is typically diagnosed in childhood, and is not preventable by lifestyle. Type 2 is linked to obesity, high-sugar and high-fat diets, inactivity, age and family history, and can largely be prevented by diet and exercise.
items.specStatementText: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
items.random_wrong: Both have the same disorder, a pancreas that has stopped making insulin, seen at an early and at a late stage of the disease.

items.q: Which change would do most to reduce a middle-aged adult's risk of developing type 2 diabetes?
items.correct: Reducing body fat through diet and regular physical activity.
items.misconception: Beginning insulin injections before any symptoms appear.
items.why: Insulin injection is the image of diabetes treatment that students have seen, and if both types are believed to be insulin shortages then injecting insulin seems the obvious answer for both. Treatment follows the physiological change. Type 1 needs insulin replacement (injections or a pump) matched to food and monitored blood glucose. Type 2 is first managed by reducing body fat and increasing physical activity, which improve insulin sensitivity, then by drugs that improve sensitivity or secretion; insulin is used only if these fail as beta cells decline.
items.specStatementText: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
items.random_wrong: Avoiding the viral infections thought to trigger loss of beta cells.

items.q: What is the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation?
items.correct: It monitors blood temperature and coordinates the responses of the effectors.
items.misconception: It passes on the core temperature measured by thermoreceptors in the skin to the effectors.
items.why: Skin is where a person feels hot or cold, so it seems the obvious place for temperature to be measured, and simplified flow diagrams show one 'receptor' box feeding one 'control centre' box. There are two sets of thermoreceptors. Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin detect the temperature at the surface, which can differ from the core by many degrees, and send impulses to the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus contains its own thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood passing through it, which is the core value that is actually regulated at about 37 °C.
items.specStatementText: Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
items.random_wrong: It generates heat itself whenever the blood flowing through it becomes too cold.

items.q: A person moves to a cold climate. After several weeks their resting metabolic rate has risen and they produce more heat even when not shivering. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: More thyroxin is being secreted, raising the rate of cell respiration.
items.misconception: The pituitary gland is secreting thyroxin, which acts as quickly as a nerve impulse.
items.why: The whole thermoregulatory response is drawn as one loop with one time scale, and students remember 'hypothalamus and pituitary' next to thyroxin without noticing that they control its release from a different gland. The hypothalamus stimulates the pituitary gland to release thyroid-stimulating hormone, and this causes the thyroid gland to secrete thyroxin. Thyroxin increases the rate of cell respiration in most tissues, so more heat is produced; because hormone concentrations change slowly, this adjusts heat generation over hours and days of cold exposure, while shivering and vasoconstriction respond within seconds to minutes.
items.specStatementText: Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
items.random_wrong: The hypothalamus has started to produce extra heat itself as the blood cools.

items.q: How does vasodilation of the arterioles in the skin lower body temperature?
items.correct: More blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, so more heat is lost to the air.
items.misconception: The blood vessels move closer to the surface of the skin, so heat escapes more easily.
items.why: GCSE diagrams show a vessel drawn nearer the surface in the 'hot' picture and deeper in the 'cold' picture, and the phrase 'blood is diverted to the surface' is read literally as vessels relocating. Blood vessels are fixed in position. Arterioles have smooth muscle in their walls; when it relaxes (vasodilation) more blood passes into the capillary beds near the surface, and when it contracts (vasoconstriction) blood is kept in deeper vessels. Capillaries have no muscle and cannot constrict; the control is upstream in the arterioles.
items.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
items.random_wrong: Warm blood at the surface is cooled by the cold sweat that lies on top of the skin.

items.q: On a hot, very humid day a runner sweats heavily, but their body temperature keeps rising. Why is sweating less effective in these conditions?
items.correct: Little of the sweat evaporates, so little latent heat is taken from the skin.
items.misconception: The sweat produced is warmer than usual, so it cannot chill the skin as it runs off.
items.why: Sweat feels cool on the skin and students associate wetness with coolness, and the energy needed for a change of state is a physics idea not usually connected to sweating. Sweat is secreted at body temperature; the cooling comes from the latent heat absorbed when liquid water becomes vapour. This is why sweating is much less effective in humid air, where evaporation is slow, and why a fan cools a sweating person: it speeds evaporation, not the sweat itself.
items.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
items.random_wrong: Humid air stops the blood vessels from moving up to the surface of the skin.

items.q: Brown adipose tissue in a newborn baby releases heat when the baby is cold. Which statement describes the mechanism?
items.correct: Protons re-enter the mitochondrial matrix without passing through ATP synthase, releasing heat.
items.misconception: The mitochondria make ATP unusually fast, and the ATP is then broken down to release heat.
items.why: Fat is taught as an insulator (blubber, subcutaneous fat), and respiration is taught as a process whose purpose is ATP, so students have no category for respiration whose product is heat and assume ATP must be the intermediate. White adipose tissue insulates; brown adipose tissue is a heat generator. Its many mitochondria carry out the electron transport chain as usual, building a proton gradient, but the uncoupling protein short-circuits the gradient so that little ATP is made and the energy appears directly as heat. This uncoupled respiration is especially important in infants and in cold-exposed adults.
items.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
items.random_wrong: The tissue forms a thick insulating layer of fat, so heat generated elsewhere in the body is retained.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes osmoregulation from excretion?
items.correct: Osmoregulation controls blood osmotic concentration; excretion removes metabolic waste.
items.misconception: Osmoregulation removes surplus water; excretion removes surplus solutes of every other kind.
items.why: Both functions are carried out by the same organ and appear in the same urine, so students merge them; and 'regulation' is heard as 'removal' because urine formation is the only kidney process they picture. The kidney has two distinguishable roles. Excretion: removing urea and other unwanted solutes from the blood into urine. Osmoregulation: adjusting water reabsorption so that the osmotic concentration of the blood stays at about 0.3 osmol L−1, which may mean conserving water (concentrated urine) or discarding it (dilute urine). Urea concentration in urine varies as a consequence of osmoregulation, not as its aim.
items.specStatementText: Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
items.random_wrong: Osmoregulation is carried out by the kidneys; excretion includes egestion of faeces by the gut.

items.q: Blood plasma has an osmotic concentration of about 0.30 osmol L−1. Red blood cells are placed in a 0.15 mol L−1 solution of sodium chloride, which dissociates fully into ions. What happens to the cells?
items.correct: Nothing visible: the solution is 0.30 osmol L−1, the same as plasma, so there is no net osmosis.
items.misconception: The cells swell, because 0.15 osmol L−1 is half the osmotic concentration of the plasma.
items.why: Concentration has previously meant mol dm−3 of the substance weighed out, and the idea that a salt separates into several osmotically active particles is met in chemistry but not linked to osmosis in biology. An osmole is a mole of osmotically active particles. Non-dissociating solutes such as glucose give one osmole per mole; NaCl gives two, so 0.15 mol L−1 NaCl is 0.30 osmol L−1, which is why 0.9% (0.15 mol L−1) saline matches the roughly 0.3 osmol L−1 of blood plasma and can be given intravenously without damaging red blood cells.
items.specStatementText: Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
items.random_wrong: The cells shrink, as water leaves them for the more dilute 0.15 osmol L−1 solution outside.

items.q: Which statement about ultrafiltration in the glomerulus is correct?
items.correct: Glucose, urea and salts all pass into Bowman's capsule, but plasma proteins do not.
items.misconception: Only urea and other toxins pass into Bowman's capsule, while glucose is retained in the blood.
items.why: The word 'filter' in everyday use means removing unwanted material, and GCSE summaries say the kidney 'filters out waste', so students imagine a sieve that recognizes toxins. The glomerular filter discriminates only by size. Blood cells and plasma proteins are retained; all small solutes pass, whether useful or not, because of the high pressure in the glomerular capillaries. The proximal convoluted tubule then reabsorbs all the glucose and amino acids and most of the ions and water by active transport and osmosis, leaving urea and other toxins in the filtrate. Two steps, filtration then reabsorption, produce a selective outcome.
items.specStatementText: Ultrafiltration, then selective reabsorption
items.random_wrong: Water and solutes enter Bowman's capsule by osmosis and diffusion down gradients.

items.q: Fluid was sampled from Bowman's capsule and from the end of the proximal convoluted tubule of a healthy kidney. Glucose was 5 mmol L−1 in the capsule and undetectable at the end of the tubule. Urea was 5 mmol L−1 in the capsule and higher at the end of the tubule. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport; urea is left behind and concentrates as water is reabsorbed.
items.misconception: Glucose diffuses back into the blood down its own concentration gradient, whereas urea is unable to diffuse.
items.why: Students think of urine as 'mostly the filtrate', not realizing that about 180 litres are filtered a day and about 1.5 litres excreted; and the role of active transport, mitochondria and microvilli in the tubule cells is not connected to the volumes involved. Reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule is selective and energy-demanding: glucose and amino acids are recovered completely by active transport (with sodium), most ions are pumped out, and water follows by osmosis, so the bulk of the filtrate returns to the blood. Urea and other toxins are left behind and so become concentrated in what remains, which is excreted in urine.
items.specStatementText: Ultrafiltration, then selective reabsorption
items.random_wrong: Urea is actively secreted into the tubule fluid, while the glucose is respired by the tubule cells.

items.q: How does the loop of Henle make it possible for the kidney to produce concentrated urine?
items.correct: Its ascending limb pumps sodium ions into the medulla, so water leaves the collecting ducts by osmosis.
items.misconception: Its ascending limb actively transports water out of the filtrate and into the tiny blood vessels of the medulla.
items.why: Students know the loop is 'for making concentrated urine' and assume the loop must therefore be where the water is removed; and 'active transport of water' seems plausible because water is what needs moving. Water is never actively transported. The loop's job is to build and maintain the high osmotic concentration of the medulla by pumping sodium ions out of the ascending limb. The collecting ducts run through this concentrated medulla, so when ADH makes them permeable, water is drawn out of them by osmosis. The loop enables water reabsorption elsewhere rather than doing most of it itself.
items.specStatementText: The loop of Henle salts the medulla
items.random_wrong: It absorbs sodium ions into the filtrate so that the urine leaving the loop is already highly concentrated.

items.q: In a healthy kidney the osmotic concentration of the interstitial fluid rises from 0.3 osmol L−1 in the cortex to about 1.2 osmol L−1 in the deep medulla. A drug blocks the active transport of sodium ions in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which prediction is best supported?
items.correct: The medullary gradient decays towards 0.3 osmol L−1, so less water leaves the collecting ducts and the urine becomes more dilute.
items.misconception: Water reabsorption in the collecting ducts continues normally, because it is driven by pumps that ADH switches on.
items.why: Students expect a hormone to 'switch on' a process and, having learned that proteins are made by transcription and translation, assume more channels means more protein synthesis; and active transport is again reached for as the way to move water. Water crosses the membrane only by osmosis, driven by the high osmotic concentration of the medulla. ADH controls whether the pathway exists: the aquaporins are already made and stored in vesicles, and the hormone triggers their rapid relocation to the membrane. Removing them when ADH falls restores a membrane that is almost impermeable to water. This vesicle shuttling allows the response to change within minutes.
items.specStatementText: The loop of Henle salts the medulla
items.random_wrong: The loop can no longer reabsorb water directly, but the collecting ducts are unaffected, so the urine is unchanged.

items.q: A person has drunk very little water for a day and their blood osmotic concentration has risen. Which sequence of events follows?
items.correct: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the rise; the pituitary secretes more ADH; aquaporins move into the collecting duct membranes.
items.misconception: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the rise; the pituitary secretes less ADH, so that water is retained rather than excreted in urine.
items.why: The name is heard as 'a diuretic hormone' rather than 'anti-diuretic', and students remember that ADH is 'about water' without fixing the direction of its effect. A diuretic increases urine output; ADH is anti-diuretic. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood osmotic concentration (dehydration), the pituitary gland secretes more ADH, aquaporins are inserted into collecting duct membranes, more water is reabsorbed and urine volume falls. When the blood is dilute, ADH secretion falls and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.
items.specStatementText: ADH and aquaporins set the urine volume
items.random_wrong: Cells in the kidney detect the rise and secrete ADH, and the collecting ducts then reabsorb more water from the filtrate.

items.q: After drinking a litre of water, a person produces a large volume of dilute urine within an hour. What has happened in the cells of the collecting ducts?
items.correct: Aquaporins have been withdrawn into vesicles, so the membrane is far less permeable to water.
items.misconception: The duct cells sensed the dilute blood themselves and stopped pumping water inward.
items.why: Because the effect is in the kidney, students place the sensor there too, and 'ADH from the pituitary' is memorized as one phrase without the hypothalamus being given a role. Detection is central, not renal. Osmoreceptor cells in the hypothalamus respond to a rise in blood osmotic concentration; the hypothalamus increases the rate of ADH secretion from the pituitary gland into the blood; ADH then travels to the kidney and acts on the collecting duct cells. The kidney is the effector, not the sensor.
items.specStatementText: ADH and aquaporins set the urine volume
items.random_wrong: Aquaporin genes have been switched off, so no new water channels are being made for the membrane.

items.q: At wakeful rest a person's cardiac output is 5 dm3 per minute, of which skeletal muscle receives 1.0, gut 1.2, kidneys 1.1 and brain 0.75 dm3 per minute. During vigorous exercise cardiac output is 20 dm3 per minute: skeletal muscle 16, gut 0.6, kidneys 0.6 and brain 0.75 dm3 per minute. Which conclusion do these figures support?
items.correct: Brain blood flow is unchanged, while gut and kidney flow fall as muscle flow rises.
items.misconception: Brain blood flow falls sharply, since its share of cardiac output drops from 15% to under 4%.
items.why: Students reason that a more active body needs a more active brain, or they over-apply the idea of 'diverting' blood away from non-muscle organs without distinguishing the brain from the gut and kidneys. The brain's blood flow is held nearly constant at about 0.75 dm3 per minute during sleep, wakeful rest and exercise, because its arterioles regulate their own resistance. During vigorous activity the extra cardiac output goes to the skeletal muscles, and flow to the gut and kidneys is reduced by vasoconstriction, but the brain is protected from both the increase and the reduction.
items.specStatementText: Blood is redirected as activity changes
items.random_wrong: The kidneys receive more blood in exercise, because 0.6 is a larger part of 20 than 1.1 is of 5.

items.q: During sleep, cardiac output falls to about 4 dm3 per minute. Which pattern of blood supply to the organs is expected?
items.correct: Muscle flow is minimal and brain flow is maintained, while the gut and kidneys still receive large shares.
items.misconception: Every organ's blood flow falls by the same fraction, because the heart is simply pumping less blood.
items.why: The circulation is drawn as one loop with the heart as the only variable component, and arterioles as adjustable resistances are not part of the GCSE picture, so the heart's output seems to be shared out in a fixed way. Arteriole smooth muscle in each organ sets that organ's share of cardiac output. In vigorous exercise muscle arterioles dilate while those in the gut and kidneys constrict, so muscle flow rises many-fold as gut and kidney flow falls; in sleep muscle flow is minimal while brain flow is maintained. Redistribution, not uniform scaling, is the rule.
items.specStatementText: Blood is redirected as activity changes
items.random_wrong: Brain blood flow falls to a small fraction of its waking value, since the brain itself is resting.

items.q: What does insulin do to glucose in the blood?
items.correct: Insulin does not act on glucose molecules at all; it binds to receptors on target cells and makes them take up glucose from the blood and convert it to glycogen or respire it, so the concentration in the blood falls.
items.misconception: Insulin is an enzyme, or acts like one, that breaks down glucose in the blood to lower its concentration.
items.why: Students learn that insulin 'lowers blood sugar' and, from GCSE enzyme work, that molecules which act on sugars are enzymes; the removal of glucose from the blood is then imagined as digestion rather than as transport into cells. Insulin is a hormone, not an enzyme. It is carried in the plasma to all tissues, binds to insulin receptors on target cells, and its effects are on the cells: increased glucose uptake, increased conversion of glucose to glycogen in liver and muscle, and increased use of glucose in respiration. Blood glucose falls because glucose leaves the blood, not because it is destroyed there.
items.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which tissues act as effectors of temperature change?
items.correct: Muscle tissues (skeletal muscle for shivering, smooth muscle of skin arterioles for vasoconstriction and vasodilation, arrector pili muscles for hair erection) and adipose tissue (brown adipose tissue generating heat by uncoupled respiration), together with sweat glands.
items.misconception: The hypothalamus itself warms or cools the body, or the only effectors are the skin and the blood.
items.why: The hypothalamus is described as 'controlling' temperature, which students read as the hypothalamus doing the work, and the skin is the organ where the responses are felt, so the tissues that actually generate or move heat are not identified. The hypothalamus is a control centre; it changes body temperature only through effectors. The guide's examples are muscle (skeletal muscle shivers, arteriole smooth muscle changes blood flow to the skin, arrector pili muscles raise hairs) and adipose tissue (brown adipose tissue releases heat directly by uncoupled respiration; white adipose tissue insulates). Blood is the carrier that distributes the heat, not an effector.
items.specStatementText: Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does hair erection warm a human effectively?
items.correct: No. Arrector pili muscles do contract and raise the hairs in cold, but human body hair is too sparse to trap an insulating layer of air, so in humans the response is largely ineffective.
items.misconception: Hair erection ('goose bumps') is an effective way for humans to reduce heat loss, just as fluffing up fur or feathers is for other mammals and birds.
items.why: The mechanism is explained using furred mammals or birds, where it works well, and students assume that any response the body makes must be useful. Hair erection reduces heat loss in animals with dense fur or feathers by trapping still air, which is a poor conductor. Humans retain the reflex and the arrector pili muscles, but the hairs are too short and sparse to trap a useful layer, so the response makes almost no difference to heat loss; shivering, vasoconstriction and brown adipose tissue do the real work.
items.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is removing faeces from the body an example of excretion?
items.correct: No. Faeces are mainly undigested food that never entered the body's metabolism; their removal is egestion. Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea and carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: Any waste leaving the body is excreted, so defecation is excretion by the digestive system and the kidney is just one of several excretory organs doing the same job.
items.why: In everyday English 'excrete' and 'excrement' refer to faeces, and GCSE treats 'waste' as a single category without distinguishing metabolic waste from undigested material. Excretion removes substances produced by the body's own metabolism: urea from deamination of amino acids in the liver, carbon dioxide from cell respiration, and other toxins. The kidney excretes urea and other solutes in urine. Egestion removes material that passed through the gut without being absorbed. Both are removal of waste but only excretion concerns metabolic products.
items.specStatementText: Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What drives ultrafiltration in the glomerulus?
items.correct: High hydrostatic pressure of the blood in the glomerular capillaries, produced because the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, forcing plasma through the fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane and podocyte slits.
items.misconception: Ultrafiltration happens by osmosis or diffusion, with water and solutes moving down concentration gradients into Bowman's capsule, or by active transport by the capsule cells.
items.why: Diffusion, osmosis and active transport are the three membrane processes students know, so any movement across a membrane is assigned to one of them; pressure-driven bulk flow is unfamiliar. Ultrafiltration is bulk flow driven by pressure. The filtrate has the same concentration of small solutes as plasma, so there is no concentration gradient to drive it and no osmotic gradient either; the plasma proteins left behind actually oppose filtration osmotically. It is the blood pressure in the glomerulus, kept high by the narrow efferent arteriole, that forces fluid out.
items.specStatementText: Ultrafiltration, then selective reabsorption
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does blood supply to the kidneys and gut change during vigorous exercise, and why?
items.correct: It falls sharply: arterioles supplying the kidneys and gut constrict so that blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles, which can receive over three-quarters of a greatly increased cardiac output.
items.misconception: During exercise the kidneys receive more blood so that the extra waste products can be removed, and the gut receives more to supply glucose to the muscles.
items.why: Students reason from what the body 'needs' (more waste to excrete, more fuel to absorb) rather than from the pattern of vasoconstriction and vasodilation that actually redistributes cardiac output. Exercise redistributes blood away from organs whose work can be postponed. Vasoconstriction in the gut and kidneys can cut their flow to a fraction of the resting value, while vasodilation in working muscle raises its flow many-fold. Waste removal and digestion resume at their full rate during wakeful rest and sleep, when the gut and kidneys again receive a large share of cardiac output.
items.specStatementText: Blood is redirected as activity changes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which direction does water move by osmosis between two solutions of different osmotic concentration?
items.correct: From the solution of lower osmotic concentration to the solution of higher osmotic concentration, until the concentrations are equal or the movement is opposed.
items.misconception: Water moves by osmosis towards the more dilute solution, because water 'goes where there is more water', or the direction is simply guessed each time.
items.why: Osmosis is often first defined in terms of 'water concentration' or 'water potential', and when the language switches to solute or osmotic concentration the direction is reversed in the student's memory. Osmosis is the net movement of water from lower to higher osmotic concentration (equivalently from higher to lower water potential). Red blood cells in a solution of lower osmotic concentration than 0.3 osmol L−1 take up water and swell; in a more concentrated solution they lose water and shrink. In the kidney, water leaves the collecting duct because the medulla outside it has the higher osmotic concentration.
items.specStatementText: Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
